newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada February trade surplus rises to C$2.19 bln.
newsitem.headline: Canada February trade surplus rises to C$2.19 bln.

text.p: Canada's merchandise trade surplus widened in February to C$2.19 million from C$1.97 billion in January (revised from C$2.10 billion), Statistics Canada said on Thursday. Exports to the world and to the U.S. hit records as did imports from the U.S.
MERCHANDISE TRADE Feb 97 Jan 97 Feb 96
Trade balance +2.19 +1.97 +2.44
Note: Figures in billions of current Canadian dollars, on a balance of payments basis, seasonally adjusted.
A Reuters survey of economists had forecast a surplus of C$2.35 billion in February, with exports of C$23.9 billion and imports of C$21.6 billion.
YEAR-TO-DATE TRADE 1997 1996
Exports 47.01 43.64
Imports 42.85 38.35
Trade balance +4.16 +5.28
Statistics Canada noted the 0.6 percent rise in exports was less than the 2.8 percent gain in January, which was also a record.
Exports to the United States, at C$19.42 billion, advanced from January's record of C$19.30 billion. Imports from the United States, at C$16.36 billion, surpassed January's record of C$16.29 billion.
Overall imports in current dollars were the second highest ever, below January's figure, though in constant dollars they were a record.
The trade surplus was well below May 1996's record of $3.80 billion.

The federal agency said machinery exports were up a robust 5.1 percent in February after two months of declines, and though aircraft shipments fell for the third month, a bevy of new orders bodes well for aerospace exports in the months ahead.

Forestry exports showed a gain of 6.4 percent, the largest increase since July 1996, countering the slightly negative trend that had prevailed since September. At the heart of the upturn was an increase in lumber sales in the United States, due to unseasonably mild weather prompting home building.
Consumer good exports rose 3.6 percent, rising for a second month, mainly due to U.S. purchases.

Offsetting much of the export gain were reduced shipments of industrial goods (-3.6 percent), energy products (-3.4 percent) and food (-2.6 percent). Industrial goods declined on lower exports of metal ores, chemicals and precious metals, offset partly by fertilizer sales.
Automotive exports fell 0.3 percent. Increased shipments of light trucks, mostly to the United States, were offset by reduced exports of cars and auto parts.
Energy imports dropped by more than 23 percent, the agency said, after having started the year at an all-time high.
Purchases of crude oil by most refiners were lukewarm and imports of refined products like fuel oil also dropped.
Outside energy, declines were marginal. Automotive and machinery imports were near record highs, the latter reflecting strength in Canadian business investment.

Continued growth in industrial goods and consumer product imports helped mitigate import declines in February. Advances for industrial goods, led by refined metals, chemicals and plastics, reflected stronger manufacturing activity. Increased demand for consumer goods reflected more liberal spending habits, it said.
((Reuters Ottawa Bureau, 613-235-6745))
